results.title: Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens | Drip
highlights:
# Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens

AI rental prices are climbing as cloud providers monetize the growing cost and scarcity of delivering usable GPU capacity.

Updated September 28, 2026

## What is this trend?

GPU rental rates are rising as cloud and AI operators pass through higher costs for power, cooling, and delivery constraints on already-contracted capacity.

- • Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI are raising prices on specific GPU offerings, not the whole market.
- • Scarcity is shifting from chips alone to deliverable capacity: power, cooling, and site readiness.
- • Utility delays and high-density racks are making retrofits and interconnects a billable constraint.
- • Operators with power and thermal control can command higher rents and better margins.
- • Pricing is fragmenting by region and SKU as guaranteed access becomes more valuable than headline supply.

## What’s the latest?

September 28, 2026

Nebius raised selected Nvidia GPU rates 17%–21%, Oracle renewed expiring GPU contracts about 20% higher, and Vessl AI lifted H100 pricing in Korea by 24.7%, where local H100 rentals were up 21.9% month over month to $3.2

results.title: DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it | Brown Forces Technology Studio
results.author: Salvador Alvarez
highlights:
# DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it

DigitalOcean just raised GPU instance prices by 20%, effective this week. The increase hits their A100 and H100 SKUs — the same chips every AI startup is fighting over. They're not the only one: Hetzner, OVH, and a handful of others have all lifted GPU rates over the past year. Supply for the good silicon is tight, and the big cloud providers have been pricing it like it's a luxury good ever since the LLM boom.

For a small shop running inference on a single A100, that's a real hit on the P&L. DigitalOcean's original pitch was cheap, predictable infrastructure for people who don't want to read a pricing spreadsheet — and this move breaks that promise. If you're training or serving models on DO, you'll want to check the new rates and compare against alternatives before committing to a long lease. The market is still hot; prices may move again.

highlights:
# Neoclod GPU Prices Surge 25% in Q2, Data Center ROI Period Shrinks to 2 Years

2026-08-31 23:52:06

According to Korea Investment & Securities analysts on August 1, neoclod companies reported significant GPU rental fee increases in Q2 results. CoreWeave implemented a 25% price increase across all products in July, while Nebius saw capacity auction prices 15% higher than previous highs. IREN's three-year contract rates jumped 125% versus November 2025, with five-year rates up 70%. Consequentially, data center investment payback periods have compressed from the traditional 4-5 years to under 2 years, with Nebius noting that $20 million per megawatt (MW) contracts now enable sub-two-year ROI, and IREN citing recent $25 million per MW agreements in negotiation.

Analysts attribute the surge to accelerating token consumption by enterprises. Google disclosed in Q2 that over 500 companies now consume 1 trillion-plus tokens, with 2,000+ consuming 100 billion tokens. Microsoft reported a 400% year-over-year increase in customers reaching annual token consumption of 1 trillion, driving higher profitability for AI model developers and intensifying data center pricing pressure.

results.title: [SMM Computing Power News] H100 rental budgets left behind, current quotes 6%–15% higher than July - Shanghai Metals Market (SMM)
results.author: Shanghai Metals Market (SMM
highlights:
Published: Sep 03, 2026 16:18 (GMT+8)

SMM learned that on July 20, a lessee with demand for renting eight H100 full servers set a budget of 71,000 yuan per unit per month. Against the current market, mainstream quotations for this model have risen to 75,000–82,000 yuan per unit per month, with the lower end of the range exceeding the budget by 4,000 yuan and the upper end by 11,000 yuan, representing increases of 5.6%–15.5%. During this period, bulk resources in north China were quoted at 75,000 yuan for a four-year closed contract and 76,000 yuan for a five-year closed contract, while annual contracts in east China reached 82,000 yuan. SMM believes that the lessee's budget has been clearly outpaced by market prices within a month and a half, and the window for low-priced H100 resources has essentially closed.

results.title: Nvidia’s price hike plan may raise India’s AI infra costs - The Times of India
results.author: Aabhas Sharma
highlights:
# Nvidia’s price hike plan may raise India’s AI infra costs

Aabhas Sharma / TNN / Sep 04, 2026, 04:39 IST

India’s AI infrastructure push could get more expensive

NEW DELHI: India’s AI infrastructure push could get more expensive. Nvidia’s reported plan to raise AI server prices by around 15% from next year is expected to increase deployment costs for GPU cloud providers, data-centre operators and companies building large compute clusters, with industry executives warning that some of the increase may ultimately be passed on to customers. The impact could be particularly significant as India scales up AI compute capacity across private data centres, cloud platforms and govt-backed programmes. Higher hardware costs could force operators to reassess expansion plans, delay fresh capacity additions or explore alternative chip architectures.“Nvidia’s pricing is driven largely by demand and component costs, especially memory, which remains tight and is projected to rise through 2027,” said Ishan Talathi, founder and CEO of CloudPe. Talathi said Nvidia had already raised prices of its RTX Pro 6000 series from $13,250 to $16,000 earlier this month, an increase of 20.8% in two months.“For an AI cloud platform like CloudPe, where GPU servers are among the biggest capex items, this translates into a 10-12% increase in overall deployment costs,” he said. CloudPe expects GPU cloud pricing in India to rise by 10-15% over the next 12-18 months unless memory supply improves or alternative architectures gain traction.

And, the pressure is not restricted to GPUs. Amit Chaurasia, data infrastructure expert and founder of Dataneers, said sharp increases in prices of memory and storage components were already affecting enterprise buying decisions.“It’s not GPUs but HDDs and RAMs that have quadrupled in price. This is an unprecedented rise,” Chaurasia said, adding that customers were delaying purchases in the hope that prices would ease. While large enterprises may have the financial capacity to absorb higher costs, smaller companies could be more vulnerable. Chaurasia said SMEs were more likely to defer technology investments, while higher hardware costs could have a cascading effect across sectors as technology becomes an increasingly important input for businesses.

results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in September 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The specialty-vs-hyperscaler spread is still ~5–7× for the identical card. What changed this month: the Blackwell B200 floor cracked below $4/hr, Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, and — the twist — AWS actually RAISED its prices while the neoclouds kept cutting. Here's the September on-demand map and the three numbers that decide which column you belong in.

...

The takeaway

- As of early September 2026, on-demand H100 rental still runs about $2–4/GPU-hr on specialty clouds (Vast.ai floor ~$1.49, GMI ~$2.00, Spheron ~$2.01, RunPod ~$2.69, Lambda ~$3.99) versus a ~$10–13/hr median on AWS/Azure/GCP/Oracle — a 5–6× spread for the identical card, essentially unchanged from August.
- H200 held or softened slightly: ~$2.30–2.60/hr at the floor (FluidStack ~$2.30, GMI ~$2.60), up to ~$6.31 at CoreWeave, with Nebius easing to ~$4.50.
- The month's real move is the B200: the on-demand floor cracked below $4 (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00, down from August's ~$4.99), spot near $2.12–2.74, and the provider field widened to 30+. Grace-Blackwell GB200 superchips also started renting by the hour (GMI from ~$8.00, Oracle ~$16).
- The twist: while neoclouds cut, AWS RAISED its H200 capacity-block prices 15% on Jan 4, 2026 (p5e.48xlarge $34.61→$39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- The decision is still utilization, not sticker: a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it's busy or not, and below roughly 40–50% duty cycle a per-token API almost always beats renting metal.

...

If you rent GPUs by the hour, the single most expensive mistake in 2026 is still the same one: paying a hyperscaler's rate for a card a specialty cloud rents for a fifth of the price. The spread is ~5–7× for the identical H100, and a month of price moves didn't close it. What did change: the Blackwell floor finally dropped below $4, the Grace-Blackwell superchips started renting by the hour — and, against the trend, AWS raised its prices. Here's the September map.

...

## The price map (published on-demand rates, early September 2026)#

Every figure below is a published on-demand rate, gathered the first week of September 2026 from public pricing pages and trackers. GPU pricing moves weekly with supply, region, and commitment — read this for the shape of the market, then confirm on the provider's own page before you commit a dollar.

- H100 (80GB) — the workhorse, and steady. Roughly $2–4/hr on specialty clouds: ~$1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), ~$3.99 at Lambda. Spot dips near $1.20/hr. Hyperscaler on-demand: ~$10–13/hr — the same card, 5–6× the money.
- H200 (141GB) — more memory, held or softened. About $2.30–6.31/hr on-demand: ~$2.30 at the FluidStack floor, ~$2.60 at GMI, ~$4.50 at Nebius (down from ~$5.50 in August), ~$6.31 at CoreWeave. Note a hyperscaler quirk: AWS's H200 via capacity blocks (~$4.98/GPU) is actually cheaper than its own H100 on-demand list rate, while Azure's H200 sits at the top of the range (~$10.60–13.78).
- B200 (Blackwell) — the month's real move. The on-demand floor cracked below $4: ~$3.70 at Spheron, ~$3.75 at Packet.ai (the cheapest in-stock rate GetDeploying tracked on Sept 3), ~$4.00 at GMI — down from August's ~$4.99 floor — with spot near $2.12–2.74 and the provider field widened to 30+. The mid-market still runs higher (~$5.50 Nebius, ~$8.60 CoreWeave), and hyperscaler B200 is ~$14–16/hr.
- GB200 / B300 (new this month) — the Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, which they effectively didn't in August: GB200 from ~$8.00/hr at GMI, ~$10.50 at CoreWeave (NVL72), ~$16 at Oracle; B300 (Blackwell Ultra) runs roughly ~$7–18 depending on provider. GB300 is still quote-only.

The headline of the month is a split screen: the cheap end got cheaper (B200 floor $4.99 → $3.70) while the expensive end got more expensive (AWS raised H200 15%). The market isn't moving one direction — it's spreading apart.

## What changed since August#

If you read last month's map, here's the delta in four lines:

1. H100 floor: flat. ~$2 at GMI/Spheron, ~$1.49 at the Vast marketplace floor. But brand-name specialty on-demand firmed — Lambda's SXM rate climbed toward $3.99, so RunPod's ~$2.69 is now a more representative "cheap-but-reliable" number than August's headline $1.99.
2. H200: stable to softer. GMI still ~$2.60, Nebius eased to ~$4.50, CoreWeave ~$6.31. No dramatic move.
3. B200: floor down, availability up. The Blackwell on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70–4.00 and the provider count roughly doubled. This is where a founder's dollar moved the most.
4. The hyperscalers went UP. AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices ~15% on January 4, 2026 (Data Center Dynamics) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades. The premium for renting from a hyperscaler is widening, not narrowing.

...

First, skip the hyperscaler on-demand rate unless you're buying the platform around the card — the gap is 5–7× and, after January, widening. Second, rent by utilization, not by sticker — a cheap GPU you can't keep busy is more expensive than an API, every time, and that's as true of a $3.70 B200 as it was of a $2 H100. Get those two right and the exact provider is a rounding error.

...

After a summer of falling floors, October pauses: H100 ~$2/hr, H200 ~$3+, the B200 in-stock floor flat near $3.75 — but a typical on-demand B200 now rents at ~$8. The floor stopped falling.

...

The hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) sit far higher — roughly $10–13/hr for the identical card. Spot/preemptible H100 can dip near $1.20/hr where offered, with no availability guarantee.

...

Did GPU rental prices go up or down since August 2026?

Both, depending where you look — and that split is the story. The low end (marketplaces and neoclouds like Vast.ai, GMI, Spheron) held or drifted lower, especially on the B200, whose on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70. But brand-name specialty on-demand list rates firmed (Lambda H100 rose toward $3.99), and the hyperscalers went the other way entirely: AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices 15% in January 2026. Net: cheap GPUs got a touch cheaper, premium on-demand got more expensive, and the spread between the two widened.

...

Why did AWS raise GPU prices when everyone else is cutting?

On January 4, 2026, AWS increased the on-demand price of its H200 EC2 Capacity Blocks by ~15% (p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU), citing supply/demand — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades, announced on a Saturday. It's a signal, not an anomaly: hyperscaler GPU pricing reflects committed capacity and platform value, not the marginal cost of silicon, so when demand for a specific part is tight, the price can rise even as neocloud spot rates fall. For a solo founder it reinforces the same lesson — the hyperscaler on-demand rate is the most expensive way to rent, and you pay it for the platform, not the card.

results.title: Rent Out a GPU Server on Vast.ai: Rates, Costs, Utilization
results.author: Viktor Bogoev
highlights:
Rent Out a GPU Server on Vast.ai: Rates, Costs, Utilization

Guides · September 2, 2026 · updated November 7 · 10 min read

# Rent Out a GPU Server on Vast.ai: Rates, Costs, Utilization

Renting out a GPU server on Vast.ai, worked through: nine weeks of median rates, the platform margin, idle power and three utilization scenarios.

By Viktor Bogoev, founder of Aura Digital

...

If you want to rent out your GPU server, the income side is arithmetic, and every term in it is knowable except one. Market rates are real and we track them weekly. Power draw is measurable: we meter the 8-GPU server we run for NEOXIS AD, in which Aura Digital EOOD is a 5% co-founder. The platform's margin shows in the gap between what renters pay and what the host receives. Utilization is not knowable in advance, and anyone who quotes you a payback period without saying what utilization they assumed is selling, not calculating.

...

Your share: since June 2024 Vast.ai charges hosts no fee and adds its margin to the renter's price instead (Vast.ai, June 2024 update). It does not publish how large that margin is. On our machine renters paid about 1.33 times our price between July and October 2026 - so for your machine to show up at the market rate, your own price has to be about 75% of it.

...

## What rates actually did: nine weeks of the market

GetDeploying publishes an open dataset of GPU rental prices across dozens of providers, with weekly medians going back a year (license: CC BY 4.0). Here is the median across providers per GPU-hour, on-demand, for the weeks starting on these dates:

| GPU | 3 Aug | 17 Aug | 31 Aug | 5 Oct | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 6.64 | 6.79 | 6.01 | 6.79 | +2% |
| H200 | 4.29 | 4.48 | 4.40 | 4.63 | +8% |
| H100 | 3.38 | 3.38 | 3.32 | 3.49 | +3% |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 2.21 | 2.19 | 2.20 | 2.20 | 0% |
| A100 | 1.87 | 1.76 | 1.76 | 1.85 | −1% |
| RTX 5090 | 0.58 | 0.46 | 0.63 | 0.70 | +21% |
| RTX 4090 | 0.44 | 0.45 | 0.42 | 0.44 | +1% |
| RTX 3090 | 0.22 | 0.13 | 0.17 | 0.22 | 0% |

Median across providers, on-demand, USD per GPU-hour; each week starts on the date shown. Source: GetDeploying, GPU rental price history (CC BY 4.0). The selection of cards is ours.

## The one interesting thing in that table

The RTX 5090 rose 21% in nine weeks. Nothing else moved like it – not its own sibling the 4090 (+1%), not the previous generation 3090 (back where it started), and not the data center cards, which moved between −1% and +8%.

But look at what else changed. In the week of 3 August, 8 providers listed the 5090; in the week of 5 October, 18 did. A median across providers moves when providers join or leave, not only when someone reprices – so part of that 21% may be about who is selling, not what they charge. Nor was the path a straight line: the 5090 dipped to $0.46 in mid-August before it climbed.

Two honest caveats. Nine weeks is a short window – four data points cannot separate a trend from a fluctuation. And these are advertised prices: GetDeploying counts every priced listing not marked sold out, which is not the same as capacity anyone actually rented at that price.

## Is Vast.ai hosting profitable? Three utilization levels

It can be, at the right utilization - and utilization is the one term we deliberately do not publish a figure for. Not because we are hiding it, but because our number would tell you nothing about yours. Occupancy depends on your region, your network, your reliability score, your price relative to everyone else's that week, and how many machines like yours came online.

So instead of a single answer, here is the same machine at three utilization levels. 8× RTX 5090, median rate $0.703/h for the week of 5 October – the unrounded figure behind the 0.70 above – 730 hours, 75% host share, electricity at $0.15/kWh, 5.98 kW when rented (8 × 575 W × 1.3) and 1.1 kW idle:

| Utilization | Gross | Your share | Power | Net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100% | $4,106 | $3,079 | $655 | $2,424/mo |
| 60% | $2,463 | $1,847 | $441 | $1,406/mo |
| 30% | $1,232 | $924 | $281 | $643/mo |

Two inputs come from our own machine rather than from a 5090 build. We have not measured an 8× RTX 5090 server at idle: the 1.1 kW is from the RTX PRO 6000 server, which has the same two EPYC 9754 processors as the 5090 servers we designed for a client. And rented hours are not all at full power. Under a real inference rental in October and November, that server averaged 2.6 to 3.5 kW, against 6.5 kW at full load, so read the power column as an upper bound for the rented hours.

That rate is the median of what providers advertise. On a marketplace you compete with the bottom of the range: the cheapest 5090 listing that week was $0.35/h. At that price the net at 30% utilization falls from $643 to about $179 a month.
